definition.text: Theodore Roosevelt’s domestic Progressive program in his second term that used federal power to regulate business, protect consumers, and conserve public lands.

anchor.quote: After the election, he moved quickly to enact his own brand of Progressivism, which he called a Square Deal for the American people.

facts.text: Public outrage over meatpacking conditions helped spur federal consumer-protection legislation during Roosevelt’s Square Deal.

anchor.quote: Alarmed by the results and under pressure from an outraged public disgusted with the revelations, Roosevelt moved quickly to protect public health.

facts.text: The Meat Inspection Act (1906) created a federal inspection and grading system for meat, including imports.

anchor.quote: The first, the Meat Inspection Act of 1906, established a system of government inspection for meat products, including grading the meat based on its quality. This standard was also used for imported meats.

facts.text: The Pure Food and Drug Act (1906) required accurate ingredient labeling and banned adulterated products.

anchor.quote: The second was the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906, which required labels on all food and drug products that clearly stated the materials in the product. The law also prohibited any “adulterated” products

facts.text: Roosevelt made conservation a central Progressive priority by expanding protected and regulated public lands.

anchor.quote: Another key element of Roosevelt’s Progressivism was the protection of public land

facts.text: Under Roosevelt, federal conservation created national monuments, bird preserves, parks, and national forests totaling about 230 million acres.

anchor.quote: In all, Roosevelt established eighteen national monuments, fifty-one federal bird preserves, five national parks, and over one hundred fifty national forests, which amounted to about 230 million acres of public land.

misconceptions.text: The Square Deal was mainly about improving wages and hours for industrial workers.
misconceptions.corrective: In this section, Square Deal reforms emphasize consumer protection (food and drugs), conservation, and regulation of railroads/business rather than primarily workplace reforms.

misconceptions.text: Roosevelt’s conservation policy aimed to lock up public land from any use.
misconceptions.corrective: The section describes conservation that preserved land but also conserved it for regulated use for future generations.

examples.text: Passing the Meat Inspection Act of 1906 after investigations confirmed conditions described in Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle.
Creating national forests and monuments to preserve public land and manage it for future use.

According to the section, which was a key element of Roosevelt’s Progressivism?
options: Ending the direct election of senators

definition.text: Theodore Roosevelt’s use of federal agencies, the Justice Department, and the courts to investigate and prosecute business trusts, distinguishing between “good” and “bad” trusts.

anchor.quote: his initial message to Congress gave only one overriding Progressive goal for his presidency: to eliminate business trusts.

facts.text: Roosevelt created the Department of Commerce and Labor (1903) with a Bureau of Corporations to investigate trusts.

anchor.quote: Roosevelt created the Department of Commerce and Labor in 1903, which included the Bureau of Corporations, whose job it was to investigate trusts.

facts.text: He pushed the Justice Department to revive prosecutions under the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

anchor.quote: He also asked the Department of Justice to resume prosecutions under the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

facts.text: The Northern Securities case reached the Supreme Court, which upheld breaking up the trust in 1904 by a 5–4 vote.

anchor.quote: In 1904, the highest court in the land ultimately affirmed the ruling to break up the trust in a narrow five-to-four vote.

facts.text: Roosevelt argued that some “good trusts” could benefit consumers through cheaper goods and services.

anchor.quote: The “good trusts,” Roosevelt reasoned, used their power in the marketplace and economies of scale to deliver goods and services to customers more cheaply.

facts.text: Roosevelt used public persuasion and prosecutions against “bad trusts,” initiating more than two dozen successful antitrust suits.

anchor.quote: In total, Roosevelt initiated over two dozen successful anti-trust suits, more than any president before him.

misconceptions.text: Roosevelt tried to eliminate all trusts and big corporations.
misconceptions.corrective: The section says Roosevelt distinguished between “good trusts” and “bad trusts,” allowing some large corporations to continue while prosecuting others.

misconceptions.text: Trustbusting was mainly done by state governments, not the federal government.
misconceptions.corrective: The section emphasizes federal tools: a new federal department, the Justice Department, and Supreme Court cases.

examples.text: The 1902 antitrust suit against the Northern Securities Trust Company.
Roosevelt’s public denunciations of “bad trusts” using the presidency as a “bully pulpit.”

definition.text: William Howard Taft’s continuation of some Progressive reforms (notably regulation and antitrust), constrained by Republican Party politics and less effective public leadership than Roosevelt.

anchor.quote: The public expected much from Roosevelt’s hand-picked replacement, as did Roosevelt himself, who kept a watchful eye over Taft’s presidency.

facts.text: Taft extended the Interstate Commerce Commission’s regulatory reach via the Mann-Elkins Act (1910) to telephones and telegraphs.

anchor.quote: He stayed the course of his predecessor by signing the Mann-Elkins Act of 1910, which extended the authority of the Interstate Commerce Commission over telephones and telegraphs.

facts.text: During Taft’s tenure, Congress proposed constitutional amendments for a federal income tax and direct election of senators.

anchor.quote: Additionally, during his tenure, Congress proposed constitutional amendments to authorize a federal income tax and mandate the direct election of U.S. senators.

facts.text: Taft initiated more antitrust suits than Roosevelt but was viewed as less skilled politically and less focused on the public good.

anchor.quote: But even though Taft initiated twice as many antitrust suits against big business as Roosevelt, he lacked the political negotiating skills and focus on the public good of his predecessor

facts.text: Taft’s decision to prosecute U.S. Steel over an acquisition angered Roosevelt, who felt betrayed.

anchor.quote: who felt betrayed when Taft took J.P. Morgan’s U.S. Steel Corporation to court over an acquisition that Roosevelt had promised Morgan would not result in a prosecution.

facts.text: Republican leaders sought to regain party control after Roosevelt, limiting Taft’s room to maneuver.

anchor.quote: Republican leaders, however, were anxious to reestablish tighter control over the party after Roosevelt’s departure, and they left Taft little room to maneuver.

misconceptions.text: Taft abandoned Progressive reforms and did not pursue antitrust policy.
misconceptions.corrective: The section explicitly states Taft initiated twice as many antitrust suits as Roosevelt and signed regulatory legislation like the Mann-Elkins Act.

misconceptions.text: Taft had full freedom to set policy because Roosevelt personally selected him.
misconceptions.corrective: The text notes Republican leaders constrained Taft, leaving him little room to maneuver and fueling conflict within the party.

examples.text: Signing the Mann-Elkins Act of 1910 to expand ICC authority to communications.
Prosecuting U.S. Steel over an acquisition, triggering conflict with Roosevelt.

kernels.term: Origins and triggers of the Spanish-American War

definition.text: The Spanish-American War emerged from Spain’s harsh repression of Cuban independence efforts, U.S. sympathy and economic/political interest in Cuba, media-driven public pressure, and the catalytic impact of the USS Maine explosion that pushed President McKinley and Congress toward war.

anchor.quote: Despite its name, the Spanish-American War had less to do with the foreign affairs between the United States and Spain than Spanish control over Cuba.

facts.text: Spain’s response to the 1895 Cuban revolt included “re-concentration,” forcing people into camps where many died from harsh conditions.

anchor.quote: Particularly notorious was their policy of re-concentration in which Spanish troops forced rebels from the countryside into military-controlled camps in the cities, where many died from harsh conditions.

facts.text: Yellow journalism by major newspapers heightened public desire for war with sensationalistic coverage.

anchor.quote: Additionally, the late 1890s saw the height of yellow journalism , in which newspapers such as the New York Journal , led by William Randolph Hearst, and the New York World , published by Joseph Pulitzer, competed for readership with sensationalistic stories.

facts.text: McKinley initially resisted starting a war with Spain over Cuba, partly because U.S. forces were untested and because of political considerations.

anchor.quote: President William McKinley, despite commanding a new, powerful navy, also recognized that the new fleet—and soldiers—were untested. Preparing for a reelection bid in 1900, McKinley was reluctant to start a war with Spain over Cuba.

facts.text: The explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor killed over 250 sailors and became a rallying point for war advocates.

anchor.quote: Just days after it arrived, on February 15, an explosion destroyed the Maine , killing over 250 American sailors

facts.text: Congress authorized force to remove Spain from Cuba and included the Teller Amendment promising not to annex Cuba.

anchor.quote: Congress received McKinley’s war message, and on April 19, 1898, they officially recognized Cuba’s independence and authorized McKinley to use military force to remove Spain from the island. Equally important, Congress passed the Teller Amendment to the resolution, which stated that the United States would not annex Cuba following the war, appeasing those who opposed expansionism.

misconceptions.text: The Spanish-American War was mainly about a direct U.S.–Spain dispute rather than Cuba.
misconceptions.corrective: The section emphasizes that the conflict centered on “Spanish control over Cuba,” with U.S. intervention framed around Cuba’s situation.

misconceptions.text: It was definitively proven in 1898 that Spain blew up the USS Maine.
misconceptions.corrective: The snapshot notes that later evidence led many historians to conclude the explosion “was likely an accident,” even though newspapers blamed Spain at the time.

examples.text: A class debate comparing humanitarian sympathy for Cuban rebels with U.S. business interests in the sugar industry as motives for intervention.
Analyzing how the headline “Remember the Maine!” shaped public opinion before a formal investigation.

kernels.term: Spanish-American War outcomes and U.S. overseas empire
aliases: Spanish-American War as imperial turning point

definition.text: The war’s rapid U.S. victory helped establish the United States as a recognized military power and accelerated imperial expansion by linking the conflict in Cuba to a broader strategy of acquiring overseas positions, including in the Pacific.

anchor.loc: 22.2 The Spanish-American War and Overseas Empire
anchor.quote: The Spanish-American War was notable not only because the United States succeeded in seizing territory from another empire, but also because it caused the global community to recognize that the United States was a formidable military power.

facts.text: John Hay famously described the conflict as “a splendid little war.”

anchor.loc: 22.2 The Spanish-American War and Overseas Empire
anchor.quote: In what Secretary of State John Hay called “a splendid little war,”

facts.text: U.S. planners approached the conflict “as a war for empire,” aiming beyond Cuba toward Pacific bases and markets.

anchor.quote: To the surprise of the Spanish forces who saw the conflict as a clear war over Cuba, American military strategists prepared for it as a war for empire.

facts.text: The first major confrontation occurred in the Philippines, where Dewey led a decisive victory with almost no U.S. losses.

anchor.quote: As a result, the first significant military confrontation took place not in Cuba but halfway around the world in the Philippines. Commodore George Dewey led the U.S. Navy in a decisive victory, sinking all of the Spanish ships while taking almost no American losses.

facts.text: U.S. forces captured Manila by mid-August 1898 and remaining Spanish forces surrendered there.

anchor.quote: By mid-August 1898, U.S. forces had captured Manilla and the remaining Spanish forces had surrendered.

facts.text: Spain rapidly lost control of Puerto Rico, offering little resistance, once its fleet was destroyed and it lacked naval support.

anchor.quote: Lacking any naval support, Spain quickly lost control of Puerto Rico as well, offering virtually no resistance to advancing American forces.

misconceptions.text: The Spanish-American War was fought only in Cuba.
misconceptions.corrective: The snapshot states the first major confrontation occurred “in the Philippines,” showing the war’s global scope.

misconceptions.text: U.S. military strategy focused exclusively on liberating Cuba.
misconceptions.corrective: The passage says strategists “prepared for it as a war for empire,” including interest in Pacific bases and expansion toward Asia.

kernels.term: African American soldiers (“Smoked Yankees”) in the Spanish-American War

definition.text: African American soldiers played crucial combat roles in Cuba during the Spanish-American War, even as they faced segregation and racism at home; their participation was debated within Black communities as both a burden under unequal citizenship and a potential path to proving patriotism.

anchor.loc: Defining American “Smoked Yankees”: Black Soldiers in the Spanish-American War
anchor.quote: The choice to serve in the Spanish-American War was not a simple one. Within the Black community, many spoke out both for and against involvement in the war.

facts.text: Nearly ten thousand African American men volunteered for service, despite segregated conditions and additional hardships.

anchor.quote: Nearly ten thousand African American men also volunteered for service, despite the segregated conditions and additional hardships they faced, including violent uprisings at a few American bases before they departed for Cuba.

facts.text: Black veterans were instrumental in Cuba; without them, the Rough Riders would likely have suffered more serious casualties.

anchor.loc: Defining American “Smoked Yankees”: Black Soldiers in the Spanish-American War
anchor.quote: But less well known is that the Rough Riders struggled mightily in several battles and would have sustained far more serious casualties, if not for the experienced Black veterans—over twenty-five hundred of them—who joined them in battle

facts.text: These Black soldiers had extensive prior combat experience from the Indian wars on the American frontier.

anchor.loc: Defining American “Smoked Yankees”: Black Soldiers in the Spanish-American War
anchor.quote: These soldiers, who had been fighting the Indian wars on the American frontier for many years, were instrumental in the U.S. victory in Cuba.

facts.text: Black regiments faced racism and harsh treatment during training in the southern states before deploying.

anchor.loc: Defining American “Smoked Yankees”: Black Soldiers in the Spanish-American War
anchor.quote: the Black regiments suffered racism and harsh treatment while training in the southern states before shipping off to battle.

facts.text: After San Juan, five Black soldiers received the Medal of Honor and twenty-five others received a certificate of merit.

anchor.loc: Defining American “Smoked Yankees”: Black Soldiers in the Spanish-American War
anchor.quote: After the Battle of San Juan, five Black soldiers received the Medal of Honor and twenty-five others were awarded a certificate of merit.

misconceptions.corrective: The text states the Rough Riders “would have sustained far more serious casualties” without the experienced Black veterans who joined them in battle.

misconceptions.text: Black Americans uniformly supported participation in the war.
misconceptions.corrective: The passage notes debate “both for and against involvement,” reflecting differing views on citizenship, obligation, and opportunity.

definition.text: Woodrow Wilson’s approach to foreign affairs that framed U.S. intervention as justified primarily by a moral imperative rather than by narrow self-interest, even as economic and strategic realities often pulled the U.S. toward intervention.

anchor.loc: 23.1 American Isolationism and the European Origins of War
anchor.quote: But he proposed an idealistic foreign policy based on morality, rather than American self-interest, and felt that American interference in another nation’s affairs should occur only when the circumstances rose to the level of a moral imperative.

facts.text: Wilson entered office promising a less expansionist approach than Roosevelt and Taft, while still believing in U.S. values and overseas markets.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: When Woodrow Wilson took over the White House in March 1913, he promised a less expansionist approach to American foreign policy than Theodore Roosevelt and William Howard Taft had pursued.

facts.text: Wilson’s administration pursued diplomacy and peace initiatives via William Jennings Bryan, including “cooling off treaties.”

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: Bryan undertook his new assignment with great vigor, encouraging nations around the world to sign “cooling off treaties,” under which they agreed to resolve international disputes through talks, not war, and to submit any grievances to an international commission.

facts.text: Despite his anti-intervention rhetoric, Wilson found it difficult to keep the U.S. out of world affairs when interests were threatened.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: Even with Bryan’s support, however, Wilson found that it was much harder than he anticipated to keep the United States out of world affairs

facts.text: In practice, U.S. policy remained interventionist when American interests were at stake.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: In reality, the United States was interventionist in areas where its interests—direct or indirect—were threatened.

facts.text: The section concludes that Wilson’s moral foreign policy efforts ran up against economic and political realities.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: Again, as in China, Wilson’s attempt to impose a moral foreign policy had failed in light of economic and political realities.

misconceptions.text: Wilson consistently avoided intervention abroad because he opposed U.S. involvement in other nations’ affairs.
misconceptions.corrective: Although he advocated restraint, the text notes the U.S. still intervened when American interests were threatened and that it was hard to keep out of world affairs.

misconceptions.text: Wilson’s foreign policy was purely about U.S. self-interest, not moral principles.
misconceptions.corrective: The text describes Wilson proposing an idealistic policy grounded in morality and intervention only under a “moral imperative,” even if practice diverged.

examples.text: Using “cooling off treaties” to reduce the chance that disputes escalated into war.
Presenting U.S. intervention as justified when circumstances reached a moral imperative.

kernels.term: Wilson-era interventions in the Western Hemisphere
aliases: U.S. interventions in Haiti and the Dominican Republic (Wilson)

definition.text: A pattern in which Wilson, despite pledging to reduce reliance on earlier interventionist policies, repeatedly used military force and control mechanisms in Caribbean and Latin American states to protect U.S. interests and enforce stability or financial obligations.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: Once president, however, Wilson again found that it was more difficult to avoid American interventionism in practice than in rhetoric.

facts.text: Wilson promised not to rely on the Roosevelt Corollary (U.S. policing role in Latin America).

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: Furthering his goal of reducing overseas interventions, Wilson had promised not to rely on the Roosevelt Corollary, Theodore Roosevelt’s explicit policy that the United States could involve itself in Latin American politics whenever it felt that the countries in the Western Hemisphere needed policing.

facts.text: Despite that promise, the text states Wilson intervened more in the Western Hemisphere than Taft or Roosevelt.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: Indeed, Wilson intervened more in Western Hemisphere affairs than either Taft or Roosevelt.

facts.text: In Haiti (1915), Wilson sent Marines after the president’s murder and the U.S. then assumed control over foreign policy and financial administration.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: In 1915, when a revolution in Haiti resulted in the murder of the Haitian president and threatened the safety of New York banking interests in the country, Wilson sent over three hundred U.S. Marines to establish order. Subsequently, the United States assumed control over the island’s foreign policy as well as its financial administration.

facts.text: In the Dominican Republic (1916), Wilson sent Marines to ensure prompt payment of a debt.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: One year later, in 1916, Wilson again sent marines to Hispaniola, this time to the Dominican Republic, to ensure prompt payment of a debt that nation owed.

facts.text: In Cuba (1917), Wilson sent troops to protect American-owned sugar plantations and the troops stayed for four years.

anchor.loc: WOODROW WILSON’S EARLY EFFORTS AT FOREIGN POLICY
anchor.quote: In 1917, Wilson sent troops to Cuba to protect American-owned sugar plantations from attacks by Cuban rebels; this time, the troops remained for four years.

misconceptions.corrective: The text explicitly states Wilson intervened more in Western Hemisphere affairs than Taft or Roosevelt and details actions in Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and Cuba.

misconceptions.text: U.S. actions in Haiti were limited to a brief peacekeeping mission with no lasting control.
misconceptions.corrective: The text states the United States assumed control over Haiti’s foreign policy and financial administration after sending Marines.

kernels.term: European alliance system at the outbreak of World War I

definition.text: The network of defense alliances in pre-1914 Europe—especially the Triple Entente and Triple Alliance—that helped convert a regional crisis into a broader war by binding major powers to mutual support.

anchor.quote: For nearly a century, European nations had negotiated a series of alliance treaties to secure themselves against their rivals.

facts.text: The two main alliances before World War I were the Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance.

anchor.quote: The two main alliances that existed in Europe before the outbreak of World War I were the Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance.

facts.text: The Triple Entente bound France, Great Britain, and Russia into a “moral obligation” to defend each other.

anchor.quote: The former bound France, Great Britain, and Russia into a “moral obligation” to defend each other in case of war.

facts.text: The Triple Alliance was a stricter mutual defense alliance including Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy.

anchor.quote: The latter was a stricter mutual defense alliance that included Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy.

facts.text: After war began, these alliances became opposing sides; the Triple Alliance became the Central powers and added the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

anchor.quote: The Triple Alliance became the Central powers and added the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

facts.text: Italy initially declared neutrality and later joined the Allied powers.

anchor.quote: Italy declared neutrality and eventually joined the opposing side, the Allied powers

kernels.term: Talkies and the rise of Hollywood’s studio system

definition.text: The late-1920s shift from silent films to sound (“talkies”), alongside the consolidation of major studios in Hollywood, expanded mass movie attendance and helped shape a national popular culture.

anchor.quote: In 1927, the world of the silent movie began to wane with the New York release of the first “talkie”: The Jazz Singer .

facts.text: By the end of the 1920s, moviegoing reached massive scale, with weekly attendance at ninety million people.

anchor.quote: By the end of the decade, weekly movie attendance swelled to ninety million people.

facts.text: Movie palaces made films accessible and affordable as mass entertainment, with a quarter covering multiple attractions.

anchor.quote: A ticket for a double feature and a live show cost twenty-five cents;

facts.text: The Jazz Singer combined new sound technology with a narrative about Americanization that resonated with audiences.

anchor.quote: It follows the life of a Jewish man from his boyhood days of being groomed to be the cantor at the local synagogue to his life as a famous and “Americanized” jazz singer.

facts.text: The Jazz Singer’s success strengthened Warner Brothers within a major-studio landscape dominated by the “big five.”

anchor.quote: It quickly became a huge hit for Warner Brothers, one of the “big five” motion picture studios in Hollywood along with Twentieth Century Fox, RKO Pictures, Paramount Pictures, and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer.

facts.text: Hollywood became the center of U.S. film production as filmmakers moved away from New York and were drawn by climate and costs.

anchor.quote: As moviemakers flocked to southern California, not least because of its favorable climate and predictable sunshine, Hollywood swelled with moviemaking activity.

kernels.term: Fordism: assembly-line mass production and the Model T

definition.text: Fordism refers to Henry Ford’s application of assembly-line mass production to make automobiles cheaper and widely available, reshaping work and accelerating consumer access to car ownership.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: Ford’s innovation lay in his focus on using mass production to manufacture automobiles; he revolutionized industrial work by perfecting the assembly line

facts.text: Ford’s assembly-line efficiency drove down the Model T’s price dramatically between 1908 and 1924.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: enabled him to lower the Model T’s price from $850 in 1908 to $300 in 1924

facts.text: The assembly line reorganized labor by moving the product between teams doing very simple steps.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: moving the product from one team of workers to the next, each of them completing a step so simple they had to be, in Ford’s words, “no smarter than an ox”

facts.text: Ford combined the moving assembly line with scientific management and time-motion studies, prioritizing efficiency over craftsmanship.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: Ford’s reliance on the moving assembly line , scientific management, and time-motion studies added to his emphasis on efficiency over craftsmanship.

facts.text: To reduce turnover from repetitive work, Ford raised wages and shortened the workday relative to common practice.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: to reduce the turnover rate, he doubled workers’ pay to five dollars a day and standardized the workday to eight hours (a reduction from the norm).

facts.text: By 1929, automobiles were widespread, with over twenty-three million on American roads.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: By 1929, there were over twenty-three million automobiles on American roads.

anchor.loc: 24.1 AUTOMOBILES AND AIRPLANES: AMERICANS ON THE MOVE
anchor.quote: Industries like glass, steel, and rubber processing expanded to keep up with auto production.

kernels.term: Stock market crash of 1929 (as trigger, not sole cause)

definition.text: A major, highly visible collapse in stock values in fall 1929 that intensified an economic downturn, but did not by itself cause the Great Depression; its impact was mediated through deeper weaknesses and resulting panic.

anchor.quote: While it is misleading to view the stock market crash of 1929 as the sole cause of the Great Depression, the dramatic events of that October did play a role in the downward spiral of the American economy.

facts.text: The crash happened less than a year after Hoover took office and signaled broader economic weakness.

anchor.quote: The crash, which took place less than a year after Hoover was inaugurated, was the most extreme sign of the economy’s weakness.

facts.text: Multiple factors contributed to the crash, and the crash helped produce consumer panic that worsened the downturn.

anchor.quote: Multiple factors contributed to the crash, which in turn caused a consumer panic that drove the economy even further downhill

facts.text: The stock market lost almost half its value in fall 1929, pushing many into financial ruin.

anchor.quote: the stock market lost almost one-half its value in the fall of 1929, plunging many Americans into financial ruin.

facts.text: Only about 10% of households owned stock, but the depression affected far more people through lost savings and jobs.

anchor.quote: only approximately 10 percent of American households held stock investments and speculated in the market; yet nearly a third would lose their lifelong savings and jobs in the ensuing depression.

facts.text: The crash alone did not cause the Great Depression; the connection involved ignored underlying weaknesses.

anchor.quote: Speculation , where investors purchased into high-risk schemes that they hoped would pay off quickly, became the norm.

kernels.term: Black Thursday and bank efforts to stop panic (Oct 24, 1929)
aliases: bank support of blue chip stocks

definition.text: The sharp one-day drop on October 24, 1929 (“Black Thursday”) that prompted major banks to coordinate purchases of blue-chip stocks to prop up prices, an effort that ultimately failed to stop the selling wave.

anchor.quote: when the New York Stock Exchange lost 11 percent of its value on October 24—often referred to as “Black Thursday”—key American investors sat up and took notice.

facts.text: The Dow peaked around 381 points in early September 1929, about ten times its early-1920s value.

anchor.quote: the Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at a value of 381 points, or roughly ten times the stock market’s value, at the start of the 1920s.

facts.text: A brief downturn on September 18, 1929 raised concerns among seasoned bankers but did not stop investment.

anchor.quote: A brief downturn in the market on September 18, 1929, raised questions among more-seasoned investment bankers

facts.text: The collapse of the London Stock Exchange on September 20 did not fully curb U.S. optimism.

anchor.quote: Even the collapse of the London Stock Exchange on September 20 failed to fully curtail the optimism of American investors.

facts.text: Leading banks coordinated to buy blue chip stocks (including U.S. Steel) to keep prices artificially high.

anchor.quote: leading banks, including Chase National, National City, J.P. Morgan, and others, conspired to purchase large amounts of blue chip stocks (including U.S. Steel) in order to keep the prices artificially high.

facts.text: The coordinated effort still failed amid the growing wave of stock sales.

anchor.quote: Even that effort failed in the growing wave of stock sales.

misconceptions.text: The 1929 crash came without any warning signs.
misconceptions.corrective: The text notes “Several warning signs portended the impending crash,” including downturns and foreign market trouble.

misconceptions.text: Big banks successfully prevented panic by buying stocks on Black Thursday.
misconceptions.corrective: The passage states, “Even that effort failed in the growing wave of stock sales.”

Placing Black Thursday in a timeline that includes September warnings and international market signals.

definition.text: The First New Deal was Franklin D. Roosevelt’s early, fast-moving package of federal programs and laws aimed at relieving suffering, promoting economic recovery, and reforming the economy through regulation, with key goals in banking, jobs, regulation, and regional planning.

anchor.quote: What later became known as the “First New Deal” ushered in a wave of legislative activity seldom before seen in the history of the country.

facts.text: Roosevelt began with a broad strategy combining short-term relief and recovery with longer-term reform through federal regulation.

anchor.quote: a combination of relief and recovery programs designed to first save the patient (in this case, the American people), and then to find a long-term cure (reform through federal regulation of the economy).

facts.text: By the end of 1933, Congress had passed over fifteen significant pieces of legislation in response to the crisis.

anchor.quote: By the close of 1933, in an effort to stem the crisis, Congress had passed over fifteen significant pieces of legislation

facts.text: Many First New Deal bills were grouped around relief, recovery, and reform.

anchor.quote: Most bills could be grouped around issues of relief, recovery, and reform.

facts.text: Initial First New Deal goals included bank reform, job creation, economic regulation, and regional planning.

anchor.quote: At the outset of the First New Deal, specific goals included 1) bank reform; 2) job creation; 3) economic regulation; and 4) regional planning.

misconceptions.text: The First New Deal was mostly a single program focused only on immediate relief.
misconceptions.corrective: It included relief and recovery but also aimed at longer-term reform through federal regulation, and it contained many separate laws and agencies.

misconceptions.text: The First New Deal primarily targeted one economic sector (like banking) rather than multiple areas.
misconceptions.corrective: It set multiple goals, including bank reform, job creation, economic regulation, and regional planning.

examples.text: Categorizing New Deal measures into relief (direct aid, jobs), recovery (stabilizing industry/agriculture), and reform (banking/financial regulation).
Explaining why the First New Deal emphasized both immediate action and structural change.

Tariff increases, annexations, currency privatization, isolationism

Doubling the gold supply, ending taxes, banning stock trading, conscription

options: Grouped around relief, recovery, and reform
Designed mainly to expand the Supreme Court

kernels.term: Emergency Banking Act of 1933 (bank holiday and reform)

definition.text: A rapid federal response to the 1933 banking crisis following Roosevelt’s bank holiday that expanded federal oversight, moved the U.S. off gold convertibility, and enabled examination and reorganization of banks so solvent banks could reopen.

anchor.quote: The resulting Emergency Banking Act of 1933 was signed into law on March 9, 1933, a scant eight hours after Congress first saw it.

facts.text: Roosevelt declared a bank holiday within forty-eight hours of taking office and called Congress into a special session.

anchor.quote: Within forty-eight hours of his inauguration, Roosevelt proclaimed an official bank holiday and called Congress into a special session to address the crisis.

facts.text: The act took the country off the gold standard and ended redemption of dollar bills in gold.

anchor.quote: The law officially took the country off the gold standard

facts.text: Gold holders were instructed to sell gold to the U.S. Treasury at a discounted rate a little over $20 per ounce.

anchor.quote: Those who held gold were told to sell it to the U.S. Treasury for a discounted rate of a little over twenty dollars per ounce.

facts.text: The comptroller of currency received authority to reorganize insolvent national banks, marking expanded federal oversight.

anchor.quote: The law also gave the comptroller of currency the power to reorganize all national banks faced with insolvency, a level of federal oversight seldom seen prior to the Great Depression.

facts.text: After federal examination, 70 percent of banks were declared solvent and allowed to reopen by March 15.

anchor.quote: By March 15, 70 percent of the banks were declared solvent and allowed to reopen.

misconceptions.text: The Emergency Banking Act permanently solved all banking problems in 1933.
misconceptions.corrective: It quelled the immediate crisis by examining and reopening solvent banks, but later measures (like Glass-Steagall) provided more permanent reforms.

misconceptions.text: Going off the gold standard meant people could still redeem dollars for gold as before.
misconceptions.corrective: The law ended gold redemption; “dollar bills were no longer redeemable in gold.”

examples.text: Explaining how a bank holiday plus federal auditing could reduce bank runs by signaling which banks were solvent.
Connecting changes in gold convertibility to expanding the circulation of paper money.

mcBank.stem: What did the Emergency Banking Act of 1933 accomplish according to the passage?
options: Took the country off the gold standard

definition.text: A set of First New Deal efforts that provided immediate assistance and especially jobs to the unemployed through direct grants to states and federally supported employment on public projects and conservation work.

anchor.quote: Roosevelt recognized that the unemployed millions required jobs more quickly than the economy could provide.

facts.text: The Wagner-Peyser Act created the United States Employment Service, offering states matching funds to create local employment opportunities.

anchor.quote: Roosevelt signed the Wagner-Peyser Act, creating the United States Employment Service, which promised states matching funds if they created local employment opportunities.

facts.text: The Federal Emergency Relief Act (FERA) authorized $500 million in direct grants to states to support relief agencies for the unemployed.

anchor.quote: He also authorized $500 million in direct grants through the Federal Emergency Relief Act (FERA).

facts.text: The passage frames these measures as combining short-term emergency help with building employment opportunities for long-term economic strengthening.

anchor.quote: These two bills illustrate Roosevelt’s dual purposes of providing short-term emergency help and building employment opportunities that would strengthen the economy in the long term.

facts.text: The Civil Works Administration (CWA) put millions to work; at its peak it employed about four million Americans on public projects such as repairing bridges and building roads and airports.

anchor.quote: At its peak, there were some four million Americans repairing bridges, building roads and airports, and undertaking other public projects.

facts.text: The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) employed young men from relief families (ages fourteen to twenty-four) for $30 per month on conservation and park-related projects; it quickly employed 250,000 men.

anchor.quote: The CCC provided government jobs for young men aged fourteen to twenty-four who came from relief families. They would earn thirty dollars per month planting trees, fighting forest fires, and refurbishing historic sites and parks, building an infrastructure that families would continue to enjoy for generations to come. Within the first two months, the CCC employed its first 250,000 men

misconceptions.text: New Deal relief was mainly cash handouts rather than jobs.
misconceptions.corrective: The passage emphasizes Roosevelt “mostly wanted to create more jobs,” including mass employment through the CWA and CCC.

misconceptions.text: The CCC was open to all unemployed people regardless of age and family status.
misconceptions.corrective: It targeted “young men aged fourteen to twenty-four who came from relief families.”

examples.text: Comparing FERA (grants to states for relief) with the CWA (temporary jobs on public works) and the CCC (youth conservation jobs).
Explaining why federal job programs could be politically attractive during mass unemployment.

options: $500 million in direct grants to states
A permanent end to bank runs

definition.text: A dominant U.S. foreign-policy stance in the 1920s–1930s that aimed to avoid involvement in European crises that could lead to another global war, even while the U.S. sometimes pursued limited international agreements and continued interventions in the Western Hemisphere.

anchor.quote: the general mood in America was to avoid becoming involved in any crises that might lead the nation into another global conflict.

facts.text: Most Americans and many prominent politicians were wary of commitments that could restrict independent U.S. action, reflecting an isolationist tradition.

anchor.quote: most Americans, including many prominent politicians, were leery of getting too involved in European affairs or accepting commitments to other nations that might restrict America’s ability to act independently, keeping with the isolationist tradition.

facts.text: Even during this noninterventionist mood, the United States continued to intervene in the Western Hemisphere.

anchor.quote: Although the United States continued to intervene in the affairs of countries in the Western Hemisphere during this period

facts.text: The Harding administration joined the Washington Naval Conference (1921–1922), which reduced navies of nine signatories.

anchor.quote: President Warren G. Harding’s administration participated in the Washington Naval Conference of 1921–1922, which reduced the size of the navies of the nine signatory nations.

facts.text: The Four Power Treaty (1921) committed the U.S., Great Britain, France, and Japan to avoid territorial expansion in Asia.

anchor.quote: the Four Power Treaty, signed by the United States, Great Britain, France, and Japan in 1921, committed the signatories to eschewing any territorial expansion in Asia.

facts.text: The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) declared war an international crime but failed because it did not require action when violated.

anchor.quote: In 1928, the United States and fourteen other nations signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact , declaring war an international crime.

misconceptions.text: Isolationism meant the United States withdrew entirely from international affairs.
misconceptions.corrective: The U.S. tried to lessen the chances of war through treaties and conferences and also continued to intervene in the Western Hemisphere.

misconceptions.text: The Kellogg-Briand Pact prevented wars because it made war illegal.
misconceptions.corrective: The agreements failed because they did not commit nations to take action when violations occurred.

examples.text: A senator argues the U.S. should avoid European disputes to prevent another world war.
The U.S. signs naval limitation agreements while still trying to stay out of European crises.

options: They required no action if violated

kernels.term: Rise of Fascism and Nazism in interwar Europe

definition.text: The emergence of one-party totalitarian regimes in Italy and Germany amid post–World War I instability and economic crisis, in which leaders dismantled democratic institutions and expanded state power through nationalism, militarism, and anti-Communism.

anchor.quote: different types of totalitarian regimes began to take hold in Europe.

facts.text: Mussolini founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in 1919 and promoted Fascism focused on national unity, militarism, social Darwinism, and loyalty to the state.

anchor.quote: In 1919, Mussolini created the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento (Italian Combat Squadron). The organization’s main tenets of Fascism called for a heightened focus on national unity, militarism, social Darwinism, and loyalty to the state.

facts.text: Mussolini articulated a totalitarian ideal: "all within the state, none outside the state, none against the state."

anchor.quote: “all within the state, none outside the state, none against the state."

facts.text: With support from industrialists and the king, Mussolini became prime minister in 1922 and by 1925–1927 turned Italy into a single-party state.

anchor.quote: With the support of major Italian industrialists and the king, who saw Fascism as a bulwark against growing Socialist and Communist movements, Mussolini became prime minister in 1922. Between 1925 and 1927, Mussolini transformed the nation into a single party state and removed all restraints on his power.

facts.text: In Germany, resentment over Versailles and fear of Communism helped the Nazis grow; by 1932, nearly 30% of the labor force was unemployed.

anchor.quote: The Nazis gained numerous followers during the Great Depression, which hurt Germany tremendously, plunging it further into economic crisis. By 1932, nearly 30 percent of the German labor force was unemployed.

facts.text: After becoming the largest party, Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933 and the Enabling Act gave him power to make laws, creating a one-party totalitarian state.

anchor.quote: appointed Hitler to the position of chancellor in January 1933. In the elections that took place in early March 1933, the Nazis gained the political power to pass the Enabling Act later that same month, which gave Hitler the power to make all laws for the next four years.

misconceptions.text: Fascism and Nazism rose mainly because Europe was stable and prosperous in the 1920s and 1930s.
misconceptions.corrective: The text emphasizes postwar recession, inflation, and the Great Depression as conditions that fueled instability and support for totalitarian movements.

misconceptions.text: Hitler became dictator solely through a popular vote.
misconceptions.corrective: He was appointed chancellor and then used the Enabling Act to consolidate power and make laws, enabling dictatorship.

examples.text: A leader uses fear of Communism and economic hardship to gain support for a one-party state.
A government removes restraints on executive power and dismantles democratic institutions.

mcBank.stem: What development helped Hitler gain sweeping lawmaking authority in 1933?

options: A growing democracy with stable parties

definition.text: A diplomatic strategy of conceding to an aggressor’s demands in hopes of avoiding war, exemplified by the 1938 Munich Pact that allowed German occupation of the Sudetenland.

anchor.quote: This Munich Pact offered a policy of appeasement , in the hope that German expansionist appetites could be satisfied without war.

facts.text: In March 1938, Hitler invaded Austria while claiming he sought to reunite ethnic Germans within one country.

anchor.quote: In March 1938, claiming that he sought only to reunite ethnic Germans within the borders of one country, Hitler invaded Austria.

facts.text: At Munich in 1938, British and French leaders agreed to partial dismemberment of Czechoslovakia and German occupation of the Sudetenland.

anchor.quote: At a conference in Munich later that year, Great Britain’s prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, and France’s prime minister, Édouard Daladier, agreed to the partial dismemberment of Czechoslovakia and the occupation of the Sudetenland (a region with a sizable German population) by German troops

facts.text: Supporters of the Munich Pact presented it as bringing peace, captured by the phrase “peace in our time.”

anchor.quote: The jubilant Chamberlain proclaimed that the agreement meant “peace in our time.”

facts.text: The policy failed to stop German expansion, as Germany soon occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia.

anchor.quote: But not long after the agreement, Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia as well.

facts.text: Stalin interpreted the British and French actions as a betrayal of Czechoslovakia and later sought an accommodation with Hitler in 1939.

anchor.quote: Stalin, sobered by the French and British betrayal of Czechoslovakia and unprepared for a major war, decided the best way to protect the Soviet Union, and gain additional territory, was to come to some accommodation with the German dictator.

misconceptions.text: Appeasement at Munich permanently prevented war by satisfying Hitler’s demands.
misconceptions.corrective: The text notes Germany soon occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia, showing the policy did not stop expansion.

misconceptions.text: The Munich Pact was mainly about reducing navies or arms limits.
misconceptions.corrective: It concerned territorial concessions in Czechoslovakia, including the Sudetenland occupation by German troops.

examples.text: A government agrees to an aggressor’s territorial demand to avoid immediate conflict.
Diplomats justify concessions as necessary for “peace in our time.”

options: German withdrawal from the League of Nations

options: Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia
Germany joined the League of Nations
Germany returned the Rhineland to France

definition.text: A decades-long struggle between the United States and the Soviet Union after World War II for technological and ideological supremacy that avoided direct military confrontation between their troops, instead relying on indirect tools like espionage, propaganda, alliances, and an arms race.

anchor.quote: The decades-long struggle between them for technological and ideological supremacy became known as the Cold War . So called because it did not include direct military confrontation between Soviet and U.S. troops

facts.text: As World War II ended, the U.S.–Soviet alliance broke down because each side believed its political and economic system was superior and their visions for Europe and the world were incompatible.

anchor.quote: As World War II drew to a close, the alliance that had made the United States and the Soviet Union partners in their defeat of the Axis powers—Germany, Italy, and Japan—began to fall apart. Both sides realized that their visions for the future of Europe and the world were incompatible.

facts.text: The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as the two postwar superpowers after traditional powers were devastated and found themselves in a broad contest for supremacy.

anchor.quote: With Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and China reduced to shadows of their former selves, the United States and the Soviet Union emerged as the last two superpowers and quickly found themselves locked in a contest for military, economic, social, technological, and ideological supremacy.

facts.text: The Cold War employed indirect methods including espionage and surveillance, political assassinations, propaganda, and alliance-building.

anchor.quote: the Cold War was fought with a variety of other weapons: espionage and surveillance, political assassinations, propaganda, and the formation of alliances with other nations.

facts.text: The Cold War included an arms race to build nuclear stockpiles.

anchor.quote: It also became an arms race, as both countries competed to build the greatest stockpile of nuclear weapons

misconceptions.text: The Cold War was mainly a direct shooting war between U.S. and Soviet troops.
misconceptions.corrective: It "did not include direct military confrontation between Soviet and U.S. troops" and was pursued through indirect tools (espionage, propaganda, alliances) and an arms race.

misconceptions.text: Only Europe mattered in the Cold War.
misconceptions.corrective: The struggle extended to influence in "poorer nations" and conflicts such as "Korea and Vietnam."

examples.text: Superpower competition carried out through espionage, propaganda, and alliances rather than direct U.S.–Soviet battlefield fighting.
Nuclear arms race between the U.S. and USSR.

options: A decades-long rivalry for technological and ideological supremacy without direct U.S.–Soviet troop combat
A brief war fought only in Europe with conventional armies
A single diplomatic conference after World War II
A trade agreement between the United States and the Soviet Union

definition.text: A Cold War strategy, articulated by George Kennan, to limit Soviet influence to areas where it already existed and prevent its political expansion into new regions, primarily through economic policy.

anchor.quote: He advised that the best way to thwart Soviet plans for the world was to contain Soviet influence—primarily through economic policy—to those places where it already existed and prevent its political expansion into new areas. This strategy, which came to be known as the policy of containment

facts.text: George Kennan’s 1946 “Long Telegram” argued that Soviet leaders saw security in destroying rival nations and their influence over weaker nations.

anchor.quote: In what became known as the “ Long Telegram ,” Kennan maintained that Soviet leaders believed that the only way to protect the Soviet Union was to destroy “rival” nations and their influence over weaker nations.

facts.text: Kennan argued the Soviet Union could not accept peaceful coexistence with the United States.

anchor.quote: He advised that the best way to thwart Soviet plans for the world was to contain Soviet influence

facts.text: Containment shaped U.S. foreign policy and military decision making for more than thirty years.

anchor.quote: formed the basis for U.S. foreign policy and military decision making for more than thirty years.

facts.text: Under Eisenhower, containment was extended into the domino theory: neighbors to Communist nations were assumed likely to succumb to Communism, like toppling dominos.

anchor.quote: American policymakers extended their strategy of containment to what became known as the domino theory under the Eisenhower administration: Neighbors to Communist nations, so was the assumption, were likely to succumb to the same allegedly dangerous and infectious ideology. Like dominos toppling one another

facts.text: To support the commitment to containment, the U.S. military and security apparatus was reorganized under the National Security Act of 1947, which created the National Security Council and CIA.

anchor.quote: the U.S. military was reorganized under the National Security Act of 1947. This act streamlined the government in matters of security by creating the National Security Council and establishing the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to conduct surveillance and espionage in foreign nations.

misconceptions.text: Containment meant immediately overthrowing Communist governments everywhere.
misconceptions.corrective: Containment aimed to limit Soviet influence "to those places where it already existed" and prevent expansion into new areas.

misconceptions.text: Containment was mainly a domestic anti-Communist policy.
misconceptions.corrective: In this section it is presented as a foreign policy strategy to restrict Soviet influence abroad, including economic policy and security reorganization.

examples.text: Using economic tools to prevent Soviet political expansion into new regions.
Adopting the domino theory assumption when assessing risks in neighboring countries.

mcBank.stem: The "domino theory" as described in the text assumes that:
options: Neighbors to Communist nations were likely to succumb to the same ideology
Communism would collapse first in the strongest industrial economies
The U.S. and USSR would cooperate through shared alliances
European recovery would happen without outside assistance

definition.text: A U.S. program (European Recovery Program) providing large-scale economic aid to European nations from 1948 to 1951 to spur recovery and counter Communist political gains, while also boosting U.S. economic and cultural influence.

anchor.quote: propose to Congress the European Recovery Program, popularly known as the Marshall Plan . Between its implementation in April 1948 and its termination in 1951, this program gave $13 billion in economic aid to European nations.

facts.text: Postwar Europe faced disastrous conditions, with slow rebuilding and looming starvation, contributing to Communist inroads in Italy and France.

anchor.quote: At the same time, the economic situation in Europe was disastrous. The war had turned much of Western Europe into a battlefield, and the rebuilding of factories, public transportation systems, and power stations progressed exceedingly slowly. Starvation loomed as a real possibility for many. As a result of these conditions, Communism was making significant inroads in both Italy and France.

facts.text: The Marshall Plan delivered $13 billion in aid between April 1948 and 1951.

anchor.quote: Between its implementation in April 1948 and its termination in 1951, this program gave $13 billion in economic aid to European nations.

facts.text: The plan required European nations to work together to receive aid, aiming to enforce unity and reduce Communist popularity in France and Italy.

anchor.quote: The plan stipulated that the European nations had to work together in order to receive aid, thus enforcing unity through enticement, while seeking to undercut the political popularity of French and Italian Communists

facts.text: Much of the aid money had to be spent on American goods, boosting the U.S. postwar economy and cultural presence in Europe.

anchor.quote: Likewise, much of the money had to be spent on American goods, boosting the postwar economy of the United States as well as the American cultural presence in Europe.

facts.text: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and forbade Communist states of Eastern Europe from accepting U.S. funds.

anchor.quote: The Soviet Union refused to accept aid from the Marshall Plan, even though it could have done so, and forbade the Communist states of Eastern Europe to accept U.S. funds as well.

misconceptions.text: The Marshall Plan was purely humanitarian and had no political or economic goals for the United States.
misconceptions.corrective: The text states Truman’s motivation was "economic and political, as well as humanitarian" and that spending on American goods boosted the U.S. economy and cultural presence.

misconceptions.text: The Soviet Union and Eastern Europe participated fully in the Marshall Plan.
misconceptions.corrective: The Soviet Union "refused to accept aid" and forbade Eastern European Communist states from accepting U.S. funds.

examples.text: U.S. economic aid intended to speed Western European recovery while reducing Communist political appeal.
Requiring cooperation among European recipients as a condition for receiving assistance.

definition.text: A major post–World War II civil rights approach that used court challenges (often supported by the NAACP) plus direct-action tests to attack segregation in transportation, housing covenants, and education, laying groundwork for later desegregation victories.

anchor.loc: 28.5 The African American Struggle for Civil Rights
anchor.quote: In the South, they used a combination of legal challenges and grassroots activism to begin dismantling the racial segregation that had stood for nearly a century following the end of Reconstruction.

facts.text: Postwar civil rights activism increasingly relied on court cases to defend African Americans’ rights.

anchor.quote: The postwar era, however, saw African Americans make greater use of the courts to defend their rights.

facts.text: In Morgan v. Virginia (1946), the Supreme Court overturned Irene Morgan’s conviction, citing the interstate commerce clause.

anchor.quote: In Morgan v. the Commonwealth of Virginia in 1946, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the conviction should be overturned because it violated the interstate commerce clause of the Constitution.

facts.text: Activists tested enforcement of the Morgan ruling through the Journey of Reconciliation, an interracial bus trip through the Upper South.

anchor.quote: This victory emboldened some civil rights activists to launch the Journey of Reconciliation, a bus trip taken by eight African American men and eight White men through the states of the Upper South to test the South’s enforcement of the Morgan decision.

facts.text: In Shelley v. Kraemer (1948), the Court held that courts could not enforce racially restrictive real estate covenants.

anchor.quote: In 1948, in Shelley v. Kraemer , the U.S. Supreme Court held that courts could not enforce real estate covenants that restricted the purchase or sale of property based on race.

facts.text: In Sweatt v. Painter (1950), the Court rejected Texas’s separate law school plan, noting inequality in facilities and “intangibles.”

anchor.quote: Texas attempted to form a separate law school for African Americans only, but in its decision on the case, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected this solution, holding that the separate school provided neither equal facilities nor “intangibles,” such as the ability to form relationships with other future lawyers, that a professional school should provide.

misconceptions.text: Civil rights gains after World War II came mainly from symbolic cultural breakthroughs, not legal action.
misconceptions.corrective: The text emphasizes that African Americans “make greater use of the courts” and highlights multiple Supreme Court decisions that targeted transportation, housing, and education.

misconceptions.text: Shelley v. Kraemer ended housing discrimination by outlawing private covenants themselves.
misconceptions.corrective: The decision limited enforcement: courts could not enforce covenants that restricted buying/selling based on race.

examples.text: Using a Supreme Court ruling to challenge segregation on interstate buses.
Challenging racially restrictive housing practices through federal courts.
Using professional school admissions lawsuits to undermine “separate but equal.”

kernels.term: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) holding

definition.text: The Supreme Court ruling that segregation in public schools is unconstitutional because separating students by race creates inequality and feelings of inferiority even if physical facilities appear equal.

anchor.quote: Marshall showed that the practice of segregation in public schools made African American students feel inferior.

facts.text: Before 1954, school segregation was required by law in seventeen states and permissible in others.

anchor.quote: Until 1954, racial segregation in education was not only legal but was required in seventeen states and permissible in several others

facts.text: Thurgood Marshall (NAACP counsel) argued Brown before a Supreme Court led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, using sociological evidence.

anchor.quote: Utilizing evidence provided in sociological studies conducted by Kenneth Clark and Gunnar Myrdal, however, Thurgood Marshall, then chief counsel for the NAACP, successfully argued the landmark case Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas before the U.S. Supreme Court led by Chief Justice Earl Warren.

facts.text: The Court noted that separation itself (on the basis of race) made segregation unconstitutional.

anchor.quote: Even if the facilities provided were equal in nature, the Court noted in its decision, the very fact that some students were separated from others on the basis of their race made segregation unconstitutional.

facts.text: After Brown, the Court ordered southern school systems to begin desegregation “with all deliberate speed.”

anchor.quote: A year later, the U.S. Supreme Court ordered southern school systems to begin desegregation “with all deliberate speed.”

facts.text: Implementation lagged: in 1960, fewer than 10 percent of southern African American students attended the same schools as White students.

anchor.quote: In 1960, four years later, fewer than 10 percent of southern African American students attended the same schools as White students.

misconceptions.text: Brown v. Board declared segregation unconstitutional only when facilities were unequal.
misconceptions.corrective: The excerpt states that even if facilities were equal, separating students by race made segregation unconstitutional.

misconceptions.text: Brown immediately integrated Southern schools at large scale.
misconceptions.corrective: The text indicates slow implementation and reports that by 1960 fewer than 10 percent of southern Black students attended integrated schools.

examples.text: Explaining why sociological evidence about harm and inferiority mattered to the Court’s reasoning.
Using “with all deliberate speed” to illustrate how legal rulings can be delayed in practice.

kernels.term: Little Rock Nine and federal enforcement of desegregation (1957)

definition.text: A 1957 crisis over school integration in Little Rock, Arkansas, where state resistance and mob violence led President Eisenhower to use federal authority and troops to enforce desegregation and protect African American students.

anchor.quote: It soon became clear that enforcing Brown v. the Board of Education would require presidential intervention.

facts.text: Eisenhower disagreed with the Supreme Court’s desegregation decision but, as president, was responsible for enforcing it.

anchor.quote: Eisenhower did not agree with the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision and did not wish to force southern states to integrate their schools. However, as president, he was responsible for doing so.

facts.text: In 1957, Central High School in Little Rock was forced to accept its first nine African American students, the “Little Rock Nine.”

anchor.quote: In 1957, Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, was forced to accept its first nine African American students, who became known as the Little Rock Nine .

facts.text: Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to block the students from attending.

anchor.quote: In response, Arkansas governor Orval Faubus called out the state National Guard to prevent the students from attending classes.

facts.text: Eisenhower federalized the Guard and sent the 101st Airborne to escort the Little Rock Nine.

anchor.quote: Eisenhower then placed the Arkansas National Guard under federal control and sent the U.S. Army’s 101st airborne unit to escort the students to and from school as well as from class to class

facts.text: This was the first time since Reconstruction that federal troops again protected African Americans’ rights in the South.

anchor.quote: This was the first time since the end of Reconstruction that federal troops once more protected the rights of African Americans in the South.

misconceptions.text: Eisenhower eagerly pushed Southern states to integrate schools immediately after Brown.
misconceptions.corrective: The excerpt says he “did not agree” with the Court’s decision and “did not wish to force” integration, but enforced it as president.

misconceptions.text: Little Rock was resolved mainly by state authorities protecting the students.
misconceptions.corrective: The text describes state forces blocking entry and federal action placing the Guard under federal control and sending the 101st Airborne to escort students.

examples.text: Analyzing a conflict between state resistance and federal enforcement in civil rights.
Explaining how federal troops were used to uphold Supreme Court rulings in the South.

options: Federalized the Guard and sent the 101st Airborne

definition.text: A conservative political turn associated with Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election and governing agenda, framing “big government” and social reform as the problem and setting policy priorities that shaped later U.S. politics.

anchor.quote: Leading the so-called Reagan Revolution, he appealed to voters with the promise that the principles of conservatism could halt and revert the social and economic changes of the last generation.

facts.text: Reagan argued that big government and social reform efforts were the problem rather than the solution.

anchor.quote: Reagan won the White House by citing big government and attempts at social reform as the problem, not the solution.

facts.text: His appeal included moderates and conservatives worried about social change and perceived decline in U.S. influence.

anchor.quote: He appealed to moderates and conservatives anxious about social change and the seeming loss of American power and influence on the world stage.

facts.text: Reagan’s election occurred amid the growth of the New Right.

anchor.loc: Republicans Back in the White House
anchor.quote: His victory was the result of a combination of dissatisfaction with the presidential leadership of Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter in the 1970s and the growth of the New Right .

facts.text: The New Right included evangelical Christians organized around issues like abortion, feminism, and sex education.

anchor.loc: Republicans Back in the White House
anchor.quote: Many were evangelical Christians, like those who joined Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority, and opposed the legalization of abortion, the feminist movement, and sex education in public schools.

facts.text: The 1980 election saw low turnout, and those who voted were disproportionately older, White, and wealthier.

anchor.loc: Republicans Back in the White House
anchor.quote: Only 52 percent of eligible voters went to the polls in 1980, the lowest turnout for a presidential election since 1948.

misconceptions.text: The Reagan Revolution describes only Reagan’s personality and communication style, not substantive political change.
misconceptions.corrective: It refers to a conservative agenda and voter coalition that shaped policy priorities and the broader political landscape.

misconceptions.text: Reagan won in 1980 because overall voter participation was unusually high and broadly representative.
misconceptions.corrective: Turnout was low, and the electorate was skewed: “older, Whiter, and wealthier than those who did not vote.”

examples.text: Linking the “growth of the New Right” to the issues emphasized by the Moral Majority.
Using 1980 turnout and demographic patterns to explain coalition-building behind Reagan’s victory.

definition.text: Reagan-era economic policy emphasizing tax cuts (especially at the top), deregulation, and anti-inflation measures, justified by supply-side theory that incentives for investment would produce growth and jobs.

anchor.quote: His economic policies, called Reaganomics by the press, were based on a theory called supply-side economics, about which many economists were skeptical.

facts.text: The policy logic emphasized cutting taxes at the top to motivate investment with downstream job creation.

anchor.quote: Reagan cut income taxes for those at the top of the economic ladder, which was supposed to motivate the rich to invest in businesses, factories, and the stock market in anticipation of high returns.

facts.text: Supporters argued growth would increase total tax revenue even at lower tax rates.

anchor.quote: Economic growth would also increase the total tax revenue—even at a lower tax rate.

facts.text: Reaganomics also included deregulation and higher interest rates to control inflation, though these initiatives began under Carter.

anchor.quote: Reaganomics also included the deregulation of industry and higher interest rates to control inflation, but these initiatives preceded Reagan and were conceived in the Carter administration.

facts.text: Congress passed the Economic Recovery Tax Act in 1981, phasing in a 25 percent overall tax reduction over three years.

anchor.quote: On July 29, 1981, Congress passed the Economic Recovery Tax Act, which phased in a 25 percent overall reduction in taxes over a period of three years.

facts.text: Despite tax cuts, government spending was not reduced, and federal employment increased during Reagan’s time in office.

anchor.quote: Reagan was successful at cutting taxes, but he failed to reduce government spending.

misconceptions.text: Reaganomics mainly targeted tax relief for low-income Americans.
misconceptions.corrective: The section emphasizes cutting income taxes “for those at the top of the economic ladder” as a key mechanism.

misconceptions.text: Reaganomics was entirely new in 1981, including the anti-inflation high-interest-rate approach.
misconceptions.corrective: The text states deregulation and higher interest rates to control inflation “preceded Reagan” and were “conceived in the Carter administration.”

examples.text: Explaining how supply-side advocates expected investment by high earners to translate into more jobs.
Connecting the 1981 Economic Recovery Tax Act to the broader Reaganomics agenda.

definition.text: A pivotal labor relations episode in which Reagan fired striking federal air traffic controllers, destroying PATCO and signaling a shift toward replacing striking workers, contributing to weakened unions.

anchor.quote: in 1981, the president fired twelve thousand federal air traffic controllers who had gone on strike to secure better working conditions (which would also have improved the public’s safety).

facts.text: Reagan’s action effectively destroyed PATCO.

anchor.quote: His action effectively destroyed the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (PATCO)

facts.text: The episode helped usher in an era in which employers replaced striking workers.

anchor.quote: and ushered in a new era of labor relations in which, following his example, employers simply replaced striking workers.

facts.text: The administration sought to weaken the power of labor unions as part of its broader approach.

anchor.quote: But Reagan seemed less flexible when it came to deregulating industry and weakening the power of labor unions.

facts.text: Union weakening contributed to the leveling off of real wages for the average American family during the 1980s.

anchor.quote: The weakening of unions contributed to the leveling off of real wages for the average American family during the 1980s.

facts.text: The strike was framed as seeking better working conditions and public safety improvements.

anchor.quote: had gone on strike to secure better working conditions (which would also have improved the public’s safety).

misconceptions.text: The PATCO episode strengthened federal unions and encouraged more successful strikes.
misconceptions.corrective: The passage states the action destroyed PATCO and encouraged employers to replace striking workers.

misconceptions.text: Reagan was consistently flexible toward unions even while deregulating industry.
misconceptions.corrective: The text says he was “less flexible” about deregulation and “weakening the power of labor unions.”

examples.text: Using the PATCO incident to explain a broader shift in U.S. labor relations during the 1980s.
Connecting union decline to wage stagnation as described in the passage.

definition.text: A post-9/11 U.S. foreign-policy stance asserting the U.S. right to protect itself from terrorism through pre-emptive war and by removing hostile governments in favor of friendly (preferably democratic) regimes.

anchor.quote: This speech encapsulated what became known as the Bush Doctrine , the belief that the United States has the right to protect itself from terrorist acts by engaging in pre-emptive wars or ousting hostile governments in favor of friendly, preferably democratic, regimes.

facts.text: After 9/11, President Bush told Congress the U.S. would bring those responsible to justice and framed U.S. policy as a war on terrorism.

anchor.quote: That evening, President Bush promised the nation that those responsible for the attacks would be brought to justice.

facts.text: Congress authorized the president to use all means necessary against those involved in the 9/11 attacks.

anchor.quote: Three days later, Congress issued a joint resolution authorizing the president to use all means necessary against the individuals, organizations, or nations involved in the attacks.

facts.text: Bush blamed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden and demanded the Taliban hand him over or face U.S. attack.

anchor.quote: Bush declared war on terrorism, blamed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden for the attacks, and demanded that the radical Islamic fundamentalists who ruled Afghanistan, the Taliban , turn bin Laden over or face attack by the United States.

facts.text: The policy included the idea of pre-emptive war and regime change in the name of self-protection from terrorist acts.

anchor.quote: engaging in pre-emptive wars or ousting hostile governments in favor of friendly, preferably democratic, regimes.

misconceptions.text: The Bush Doctrine only meant retaliating after an attack had already occurred.
misconceptions.corrective: In the text, the doctrine is explicitly tied to "pre-emptive wars" and "ousting hostile governments" as forms of self-protection.

misconceptions.text: The Bush Doctrine was only about Afghanistan and had nothing to do with broader U.S. strategy.
misconceptions.corrective: The definition frames it as a general belief about U.S. rights and tools (pre-emption and regime change), not a single-country policy.

examples.text: Explaining how the Bush Doctrine justified action against governments seen as harboring or supporting terrorists.
Comparing a pre-emptive war rationale to a traditional deterrence or containment rationale.
