definition.text: A coordinated terrorist operation on September 11, 2001 in which al-Qaeda hijackers seized four U.S. airliners, struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, and caused a fourth plane to crash in Pennsylvania after passengers intervened.

anchor.quote: Shortly after takeoff on the morning of September 11, 2001, teams of hijackers from the Islamist terrorist group al-Qaeda seized control of four American airliners.

facts.text: Two hijacked planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan.

anchor.quote: Two of the airplanes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan.

facts.text: Both towers collapsed within two hours due to crash heat and burning jet fuel, becoming rubble.

anchor.quote: Less than two hours later, the heat from the crash and the explosion of jet fuel caused the upper floors of both buildings to collapse onto the lower floors, reducing both towers to smoldering rubble.

facts.text: The Pentagon attack killed everyone on board the plane and 125 people on the ground.

anchor.quote: The third hijacked plane was flown into the Pentagon building in northern Virginia, just outside Washington, DC, killing everyone on board and 125 people on the ground.

facts.text: The fourth plane crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania after passengers tried to storm the cockpit; all aboard died.

anchor.quote: The fourth plane, also heading towards Washington, crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, when passengers, aware of the other attacks, attempted to storm the cockpit and disarm the hijackers. Everyone on board was killed

misconceptions.text: All four hijacked planes reached their intended targets.
misconceptions.corrective: The text states the fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to regain control.

misconceptions.text: The 9/11 attacks were carried out by a domestic U.S. group rather than an international terrorist organization.
misconceptions.corrective: The snapshot identifies "the Islamist terrorist group al-Qaeda" as the group whose hijackers seized the planes.

examples.text: Tracing how the sequence of hijackings created multiple simultaneous crisis sites (New York, Virginia, Pennsylvania).
Discussing how live media coverage shaped public perception of the second World Trade Center impact.

definition.text: The 2003 U.S.-led coalition invasion of Iraq launched after the United States cut off relations with Iraq, justified publicly in part by fears about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and claims of UN resolution violations.

anchor.quote: Two days later, in a coalition with Great Britain, Australia, and Poland, the United States began “Operation Iraqi Freedom” with an invasion of Iraq.

facts.text: A faction in the Bush administration labeled neoconservatives pushed for striking Iraq in the wake of 9/11; others like Colin Powell were more cautious.

anchor.quote: A faction within the Bush administration, sometimes labeled neoconservatives, believed Iraq’s recalcitrance in the face of overwhelming U.S. military superiority represented a dangerous symbol to terrorist groups around the world

facts.text: A key argument for invasion was fear that Saddam Hussein was stockpiling weapons of mass destruction (nuclear, chemical, or biological).

anchor.quote: The immediate impetus to the invasion, it argued, was the fear that Hussein was stockpiling weapons of mass destruction ( WMDs ): nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons capable of wreaking great havoc.

facts.text: Hans Blix dismissed U.S. claims of Iraqi WMD possession, arguing Iraq did not appear to have WMDs.

anchor.quote: Hans Blix, dismissed these claims. Blix argued that while Saddam Hussein was not being entirely forthright, he did not appear to be in possession of WMDs.

facts.text: The U.S. began the invasion after cutting off relations with Iraq and building a coalition including Great Britain, Australia, and Poland.

anchor.quote: On March 17, 2003, the United States cut off all relations with Iraq. Two days later, in a coalition with Great Britain, Australia, and Poland

facts.text: Though early military progress seemed smooth, the U.S. was not prepared for long occupation and conflict, making the 2003 victory celebration premature by more than seven years.

anchor.quote: Thus, even though Bush proclaimed a U.S. victory in May 2003, on the deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln with the banner “Mission Accomplished” prominently displayed behind him, the celebration proved premature by more than seven years

misconceptions.text: The Iraq War was universally supported within the Bush administration.
misconceptions.corrective: The text describes internal debate, noting some officials pushed for war while others, including Colin Powell, were more cautious.

misconceptions.text: The Iraq invasion quickly ended with no long-term occupation problems.
misconceptions.corrective: The section states the U.S. was unprepared for occupation and ensuing law-and-order and sectarian conflicts, and that the victory celebration was premature.

examples.text: Evaluating how WMD claims and UN-resolution arguments were used to justify the 2003 invasion.
Analyzing why early battlefield success did not translate into stable post-invasion governance.
